messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mere is a 66-year-old Fijian-American woman, widowed, who works as a network engineer at a mid-sized telecommunications firm. She presented for psychological assessment following a referral from her primary care physician, who had grown concerned about significant weight loss and social withdrawal over the preceding eighteen months. Mere's PCL-5 score of 75 places her in a range indicating severe posttraumatic symptomatology, and the clinical picture that emerged across the intake and early sessions is one of a woman whose inner world has been profoundly reorganised by an assault she experienced at a work function approximately two years ago.

The event occurred at an after-hours networking event held at a hotel conference suite. A male colleague, who had been drinking heavily, cornered Mere in a corridor adjacent to the main hall. The smell of alcohol on his breath was the last thing she registered clearly before he grabbed her, pressed her against the wall, and assaulted her. She did not call out. She did not fight him off. She stood frozen, and when it was over she straightened her jacket and returned to the room, telling no one. It is this moment — the freezing, the silence, the returning to the room — that has since become the source of some of the most corrosive material in her presentation. Mere had come to believe, with quiet but absolute conviction, that she had acted in ways that went against everything she understood herself to be. She felt ashamed of what had been done to her body and was certain that her passivity had proven something damning about her character. Alongside this sat a helplessness she could not reason her way out of: the world had shown her that bad things could happen to her without warning and without recourse, and no subsequent reassurance had been able to dislodge that knowledge. These appraisals did not remain abstract. They sharpened her sensitivity to the very cues that had been present during the assault — the smell of alcohol at a colleague's desk, a friendly arm around her shoulders in the break room, a younger engineer leaning in to speak quietly to her — so that each of these moments arrived not as ordinary social contact but as something charged and dangerous.

At work, where Mere spends long hours in open-plan offices and occasionally attends team lunches, the environment has become a landscape she navigates with sustained vigilance. She finds herself scanning meeting rooms for objects that could be used as weapons, registering the weight and placement of a stapler, a glass, a laptop charger. When a colleague touches her arm unexpectedly — something that happens casually in a busy office — she startles with a force that embarrasses her, and she has come to believe, despite what anyone tells her, that she cannot trust that she is safe in any environment. This state of sustained threat monitoring has made the ordinary texture of her working day exhausting, and over time it has driven her to organise her life around reducing exposure. She has declined team events. She has stopped accepting invitations to lunch. She has begun eating very little, controlling her food intake with a rigidity that feels, to her, like the one domain in which she retains authority over her own body. She gave up the community choir she had sung in for eleven years. She has kept everyone — colleagues, her adult children, old friends — at careful emotional distance, understanding that closeness of any kind now carries the texture of threat.

What has made this harder to interrupt is that the strategies themselves have begun to feed back into the very appraisals driving them. The withdrawal and self-restriction confirm, in Mere's experience, that she is someone diminished — someone who can no longer trust herself to manage ordinary human contact. And as her world has narrowed, the remaining cues have grown more potent: the smell of wine at a family dinner, a daughter's embrace at the door, a friend's hand on her arm. Each encounter with these cues sends her back toward restriction and avoidance, tightening a loop she has not, until now, been able to name.

What finally brought Mere to seek help was her daughter's tearful observation, at Christmas, that she no longer recognised her mother. Mere arrived at the first session composed and precise, the way she is at work. What she said she most feared was that the woman she had been before was simply gone. What she said she most hoped for, quietly, was that this might not be true.
